payload.body: Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

payload.body: Lexeme is a human-made conceptual category — the minimal meaningful unit of a language that functions as the basic item in the mental lexicon of speakers. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimal meaningfulness: the lexeme carries semantic content that cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful parts within that language's grammar, distinguishing it from phrases or complex words whose meaning is compositional; (2) identity-independence: the lexeme has a single abstract identity across all its surface forms — inflectional variants (walk/walks/walked/walking) and allomorphic variants (happy/happiness) express the same lexeme, while a shift in core meaning or derivational structure marks a different lexeme; (3) mental reality: lexemes are stored and retrieved by speakers as discrete units in the mental lexicon, not as lists of word forms. Lexemes persist as the atomic referent of grammatical description, lexical semantics, and word-formation rules. payload.body: Neurolinguistics is a human-made interdisciplinary field — the study of the neural and biological mechanisms that underlie language acquisition, processing, representation, and comprehension. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory level is biological/neural (brain anatomy, neural circuits, electrophysiological responses, neuroimaging data, lesion studies, and molecular markers), not purely behavioral or computational; (2) the phenomenon explained is language in its full range — phonology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, lexicon, acquisition, and breakdown — treated as operations implemented by neural systems. Neurolinguistics persists as an active research enterprise that generates testable hypotheses about how the brain implements language, uses these hypotheses to interpret clinical conditions (aphasia, dyslexia, speech disorders), and informs brain-computer interfaces for language restoration. Paradigmatic methods: fMRI and EEG mapping of language tasks, lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients, intracranial electrophysiology, and computational modeling of neural language processing. [formal: neurolinguistica | substrate: brain | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Cognitive-linguistics is a human-made approach to linguistics — the study of language as a manifestation of general cognitive abilities, including categorization, conceptualization, metaphorical reasoning, and embodied experience. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory framework denies that language operates as an autonomous module separate from general cognition; language structure reflects domain-general cognitive mechanisms like attention, memory, pattern recognition, and conceptual blending; (2) the empirical evidence comes from cross-linguistic analysis of how semantic structure, syntactic patterns, and figurative language systematically reflect cognitive universals (spatial reasoning, embodiment, force-dynamics) rather than language-internal formal rules. Cognitive-linguistics persists as a theoretical framework that produces models of construction grammar, conceptual metaphor theory, and cognitive semantics, generating testable predictions about language use, acquisition, and processing that compete with modularist accounts. Paradigmatic cases: conceptual metaphor analysis (e.g., ARGUMENT IS WAR), construction grammar descriptions, image-schema theory. [formal: cognitio-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Corpus-linguistics is a human-made empirical approach to linguistics — the study of language patterns, structures, and usage through systematic analysis of large, representative collections of real-language data (corpora). Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the primary data source is authentic, naturally occurring language recorded in written or spoken form (not introspective or constructed examples), organized into annotated or searchable text collections that sample from defined populations, registers, genres, or time periods; (2) the analytical methods are data-driven and statistical, including frequency analysis, collocation measurement, concordance line examination, n-gram modeling, and distributional semantics, used to discover patterns that may not be predictable from theory alone. Corpus-linguistics persists as a methodological framework that generates empirical descriptions of language (dictionaries, grammars), tests theoretical hypotheses against real usage data, and produces applications in language technology (spell checkers, machine translation, language models), lexicography, and language education. Paradigmatic cases: Brown Corpus frequency analysis, COCA/COHA diachronic corpora, Sketch Engine collocation tools. [formal: corpus-linguistica | substrate: data | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory.
